p.x:
My grandpa loves newspapers. Every morning, he walks to the shop and buys a daily paper. He also buys a weekly magazine on Fridays.
First, he looks at the front page. Then he reads the sports page, because he loves football. He always checks the weather report before he goes out.
I don't read newspapers. I read comics, and I watch the TV news with my dad in the evening. Grandpa says, "Be careful! Some stories on the internet are false." He's right.

Fifty years ago, most people got their news from a newspaper. A paperboy delivered it to the door early in the morning, or people bought one from the newsagent. Many readers checked the local news, their horoscope and the crossword. The ink often left black marks on their fingers!
Today, things are very different. Many young people never buy a paper. Instead, they watch videos, follow a blogger, or see what is trending on social media. When something big happens, breaking news appears on their phones within seconds. Some people still like to watch a newsreader on TV in the evening.
Good journalists work hard to find the truth. They investigate stories, interview an eyewitness, and attend a press conference where a spokesperson answers questions. A reporter who finds an important story before anyone else gets a scoop. A columnist, on the other hand, writes about their own opinions. Readers can reply by writing a letter to the editor.
However, not all news is reliable. Some reports are biased, showing only one side of the story, while good news should be neutral. Fake news is a growing problem. Because many newspapers are losing money, they now put articles behind a paywall, so readers need a subscription to read them.

Journalism has often been described as a watchdog, holding governments and corporations to account. Some of history's most important stories were exposed by reporters who relied on a whistle-blower, an insider willing to reveal wrongdoing despite the risk to their career. Sources sometimes speak off the record, meaning their names will not be published, and protecting them is a fundamental principle of journalism.
Yet press freedom is under pressure worldwide. In some countries, journalists who criticise those in power face imprisonment or violence. Elsewhere, the threat is more subtle: powerful individuals may use libel laws to silence reporters, even when the reporting is accurate. Governments, meanwhile, employ teams of advisers whose job is to put a positive spin on bad news.
The digital revolution has created both opportunities and dangers. Citizen journalism, in which ordinary people record and share events on their smartphones, has brought attention to stories that traditional media might have missed. At the same time, deliberate disinformation spreads faster than ever. Algorithms tend to show users content that matches their existing beliefs, trapping many in an echo chamber where opposing views rarely appear.
Traditional newspapers have struggled to adapt. Broadsheets, once the main source of serious news, have seen their sales fall dramatically. In response, many news organisations have invested in teams that fact-check claims made by politicians and viral posts. Experts agree that, in this environment, readers too must take responsibility for questioning what they read.
